newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo monetary policy relaxed but seen stabilising.
newsitem.headline: Yugo monetary policy relaxed but seen stabilising.

text.p: Yugoslavia relaxed its monetary policy in the last quarter of 1996 but is expected to stabilise in next month or two, analysts said on Wednesday.

"Monetary policy, moderately restrictive from April to September, was relaxed significantly in the last quarter of the year, especially in December," Slobodan Milisavljevic, an economist of the Belgrade-based Market Research Institute (IZIT) told Reuters.

"I expect it to stabilise at this level at least for a month or two," he said adding that everything depends on the political situation in the country, where opposition protests over election fraud have entered their 11th week.
"In extraordinary situation like it is now, the government faces some unpredictable costs," he said, suggesting the government must make extra payouts to the police used during the citizens protests.
"This was not envisaged in the budget, but must be paid," he said.
IZIT estimated M1 rose about 740 million dinars ($135.5 million) to 5.75 billion dinars by the end of last December, up 15 percent against the previous month.
In September M1 stood at 4.596 billion dinars, in October it was 5.04 billion dinars and in November it fell by 0.7 percent over the previous month.
The official central bank data for December M1 was not yet available, but Milisavljevic said that was normal whenever there was a substantial increase in the money supply.
In the last three months of 1996, M1 rose at average by eight percent each month against 5.3 percent average monthly rise from April to September.
IZIT estimate that the money in circulation represented the lion's share of about 54-55 percent of December M1, up 23 percent against November.
"The enormous amount of money in circulation is obviously linked to pension and late wages payouts," said Tomislav Milosavljevic, another IZIT economist.
Moderately restrictive monetary policy from April to September produced good results, increasing industrial output and stabilising market and prices.
Analysts said that the worrying relaxation of monetary policy and the rise in M1 was not followed by an increase of production or rise in foreign currency reserves.
December production declined two percent from the previous month, and November fell 7.2 percent from October.
"More money in circulation only encourages further violations of financial discipline and widely opens doors for cash to enter illegal channels," Milosavljevic said.
The extra money was not used to restart idle production, nor did it improve solvency. It hit the streets, destabilising the local currency and boosting the black market exchange rate.

The dinar plunged to 4.3 to the German mark in the week of January 6 on a sudden flood of notes put into circulation during the last few days of 1996 before the eight-day New Year and Christmas holidays.

Some analysts blamed the Serbian government for putting pressure on the central bank to print the money to ensure payouts. Others said the money was needed to cover huge imbalances of the two largest commercial banks. Some blamed the debtors' lobby.

"Whoever did it and for what ever reason, it proved that political influences are still very strong here," Milisavljevic said. "And latent danger of another attack on dinar is permanently in the air."
($1=5.46 dinars)
